extracted.intended_audience: aspiring science fiction and fantasy writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting, revising, and publishing speculative fiction (science fiction and fantasy), covering storycraft (plot, character, dialogue), worldbuilding, technical plausibility, comedy, submissions, and the market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft and market tales of the fantastic
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring expert advice on how to craft and market tales of the fantastic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book promises both craft-focused guidance and practical publishing/market advice; effective work must attend to story quality and to how to get the story published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft believable stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice from award-winning writers on 'how to craft believable stories.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Believability includes internal consistency of worldbuilding, credible characters, and plausible cause-and-effect within the speculative premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeing your way to better stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Stanley Schmidt's essay aimed at improving a writer's ability to visualize and structure stronger stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on clarity of concept and seeing the story's arc from idea to execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: You and Your Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop strong, well-motivated characters and understand their relation to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character-driven considerations: voices, motivations, development across the arc, and how characters embody theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use everyday and cultural detail for worldbuilding ('You Are What You Eat')
rubrics_metrics.description: From 'Living the Future: You Are What You Eat' — use quotidian details (e.g., diet) to convey culture and future life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, specific details can make a speculative world feel lived-in and plausible; choose details that reveal social structure, technology, and values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques and editorial guidance on writing effective dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make dialogue serve character and plot, avoid info-dumps, ensure distinct voices, and use subtext; see Asimov's editorial pieces for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: Essay(s) on plotting mechanics and structuring stories for impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice covers pacing, cause-and-effect, plotting devices to maintain reader engagement, and avoiding contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: On the writing of speculative fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Heinlein's classic guidance on principles specific to speculative fiction craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General craft maxims and genre-specific expectations (economy, clarity, plausibility) that have stood as long-term advice for writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding and understanding clichés ('The Ideas That Wouldn't Die')
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and avoid overused tropes and 'awful clichés' that feel unoriginal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the clichés of the field and the circumstances under which an experienced writer can nevertheless 'get away with' them; strive for fresh treatment or purposeful subversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning to write comedy in SF/F
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques for writing humor: 'Learning to Write Comedy or Why It's Impossible and How to Do It' (Connie Willis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy in speculative fiction requires timing, juxtaposition of the fantastic with the mundane, and genre-aware punchlines; it's challenging but teachable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good writing is not enough
rubrics_metrics.description: A reminder that excellent prose alone won't guarantee publication or success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers must also consider market expectations, professionalism in submissions, and other non-style factors that influence editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worldbuilding: creation of imaginary worlds
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical and imaginative approaches to building convincing worlds ('The World Builder's Handbook and Pocket Companion').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes dense, technical considerations (axial tilt, luminosity, chemistry) for hard-SF plausibility; tailor detail level to reader interest and story needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of imaginary beings
rubrics_metrics.description: How to design believable non-human characters and species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider biology, ecology, cognition, social organization, and how alien beings' perspectives affect narrative choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to build a future / Building a starfaring age
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing plausible futures and large-scale societal/civilizational developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think through technological, economic, political, and cultural trajectories; scale consistency and cause-effect across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of math and science for realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice that settings and alien characters should be 'scientifically plausible'; use math and science to make realistic stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate technical detail can enhance credibility; however, avoid overloading fiction with equations or graphs unless appropriate for audience and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Mechanics of Submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical advice on submitting work: 'helpful hints on getting your story out of the slush pile and into print.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes manuscript preparation, submission etiquette, format and cover letter expectations, and understanding editorial preferences. Note: some specific market details in older essays may be outdated—check current guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategies and processes for revising and improving manuscript drafts ('Revisions' — Asimov's Editorials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision is a distinct craft step: structural edits, cutting, tightening prose, and responding to feedback; iterative reworking is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing for young people
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapting content, tone, and complexity for younger readers ('Writing for Young People' — Asimov's Editorials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider age-appropriate themes, language, pacing, and moral framing when writing YA or children's speculative fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice for new writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical tips targeting beginners ('New Writers' — Asimov's Editorials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers basics of craft, persistence, common beginner pitfalls, and how to approach the submission process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors vs. Editors — understand editorial perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Insights on the author-editor relationship and what editors look for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn editorial priorities (marketability, clarity, originality), how to respond professionally to rejections and edits, and how to avoid behaviors that 'annoy editors.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the market / market listings
rubrics_metrics.description: Information about publication markets and where to submit ('Market Listings').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should research and target appropriate markets; be aware that market information ages—verify current submission practices and pay rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read contemporary work
rubrics_metrics.description: Asimov's tip: 'Read as much contemporary science fiction as possible so that you will learn what science fiction is all about right now.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping up with current genre trends helps writers understand reader expectations and market tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write consistently/practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Asimov's tip: 'Write as much science fiction as possible because you need the practice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent writing builds craft, helps find voice, and produces material for submission and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate a thick skin / resilience
rubrics_metrics.description: Asimov's tip: 'Cultivate a very thick skin so that you will survive the disappointment and fructation you will undoubtedly have to cope with.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect rejection and criticism; use feedback constructively and persevere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor technical detail to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overloading fiction with excessive technical graphs/equations unless suited to reader and story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some essays are 'too many graphs and equations' for casual readers; balance depth of technical explanation with readability and narrative needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update dated business/submission advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Many essays on submission and market are dated (typewriter-era specifics); readers must check for current practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat older submission mechanics as general principles but verify modern procedures (e.g., electronic submissions, current market outlets) before acting on specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize genre balance (SF vs Fantasy emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The collection is 'light on fantasy' and heavier on SF technical/worldbuilding essays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers primarily focused on fantasy may need supplemental resources focused on mythic/world-magic systems and genre-specific conventions.
